summary: Defines extensions to FTP that add optional security, such as authentication and protection of the data and commands sent over a connection. These are new commands and replies that clients and servers can negotiate.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2228 adds optional commands to the File Transfer Protocol so that a client and a server can prove who they are, protect commands from being altered, and encrypt the file data. A client names a security mechanism, the two sides exchange the data that mechanism needs, and later commands say how the command and data channels should be protected. The actual cryptography is left to the security mechanism, and the memo keeps the change compatible with the original FTP specification.

what is the ftp auth command
what does ftp prot command do
subtitle: Optional FTP commands that add authentication, integrity and encryption to the control and data channels.

tldr.problem: The File Transfer Protocol sends usernames and passwords in cleartext, and offers no way to prove the identity of the server, to detect altered commands, or to protect the file data itself. Anyone watching the network can read the password and change the transfer.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds optional commands to FTP. AUTH names a security mechanism, ADAT carries the mechanism's data to build a security association, and further commands protect the command channel and the data channel. All of the security work is done by the chosen mechanism, so the memo defines the plumbing rather than the cryptography.
tldr.outcome: The extensions are compatible with RFC 959 and change no existing command, but none of them is required, so a server can still refuse them. The memo also states what they cannot do: they cannot secure a transfer between two servers, because there is no control connection between servers to carry the tokens.

facts.label: New FTP commands
facts.value: 8: AUTH, ADAT, PROT, PBSZ, CCC, MIC, CONF, ENC

facts.label: PROT levels
facts.value: C clear, S safe, E confidential, P private

facts.label: Data block length prefix
facts.value: Four byte unsigned integer, most significant byte first

today: RFC 2228 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level. It updates RFC 959, the File Transfer Protocol, by adding optional commands and leaves every existing command untouched, and it has not been obsoleted. Its own appendices specify the GSS-API and Kerberos version 4 mechanisms.

sections.title: Why FTP Needed Security Extensions
sections.content:
The File Transfer Protocol as defined in STD 9, RFC 959, authenticates clients with a username and a password passed in cleartext by the USER and PASS commands. Apart from anonymous archives, that is a security risk, because the password can be stolen by watching the local or wide-area network. It also limits the files that servers are willing to publish.

Authenticating the client is only part of the problem. FTP has no way to authenticate the server, to protect sensitive data, or to verify that the data arrived unaltered. An attacker who only watches the network can read the transferred data; an active attacker can delete or modify it, start spurious transfers to a site of the attacker's choosing, and run other commands on the server. The memo notes that these security services have value even for anonymous file access.

Secure file transfer was being done in ways the memo dismisses as no more than de facto practice and none of them interactive: sending files by FTP that were encrypted beforehand under manually distributed keys, sending encrypted files by electronic mail, sending PEM messages, or using the rcp command enhanced with Kerberos. The memo argues that security services introduced into FTP need to be interoperable and should reuse existing security infrastructure, which means extending the protocol itself.

Two alternatives are considered and rejected. The FTP control connection follows the Telnet protocol, and Telnet defines an authentication and encryption option, but RFC 1123 explicitly forbids Telnet option negotiation over the control connection other than Synch and IP. The Telnet option also does not provide integrity protection alone, and does not address the data channel at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain FTP sends the password in the clear and gives no way to check that the server is genuine or that the data was not changed on the way. Sending encrypted files by other means worked, but none of those ways was interactive or agreed on. The memo therefore extends FTP itself, and rules out the Telnet option because the host requirements document forbids negotiating it on the control connection.

sections.title: The Security Model
sections.content:
At the highest level the extensions provide an abstract mechanism for authenticating connections and for protecting commands, replies and data transfers with integrity and confidentiality. The security mechanism itself is a separate piece of work: the memo defines how the client and server use it, and what the resulting protections mean.

An FTP security interaction starts when the client sends AUTH to name the security mechanism it wants. The server accepts it, rejects it, or, if it does not implement the extensions at all, rejects the command. The client may try several mechanisms until one is accepted, which gives a rudimentary negotiation. If the server needs more information, the client and server run a security data exchange: the client sends ADAT with the first block of security data, the server's reply says whether the exchange is complete, whether there was an error, or whether more data is needed, and the server's reply may carry security data back. The exchange repeats as often as necessary, and when it finishes the two sides have a security association.

The memo is careful about what a security association means. It may include authentication of the client, of the server, or of both, and keying material for integrity or confidentiality, depending on the mechanism. The purpose of the data exchange is to establish that association, which might not include any authentication at all: a Diffie-Hellman exchange establishes a secret key but authenticates nobody. If the server has an RSA key pair and the client does not, the client can authenticate the server but the server cannot authenticate the client.

Once the association exists, the authentication it carries may be used instead of, or in addition to, the ordinary username and password exchange used to authorize a user. A username given by the USER command is always required, to name the identity to use on the server.

The memo does not specify policy. Implementations may restrict what may be done depending on the security association in force. A server may require the client to authorize through a security mechanism rather than with a password, require a one-time password from a token, require at least integrity protection on the command channel, or require that certain files be transmitted encrypted. A client may refuse to transfer files without integrity protection, to be sure the files it received are valid.

No particular set of functionality is required of a mechanism, beyond the dependencies among the commands. A mechanism that provides only integrity protection, or one-way authentication, or encryption with no authentication at all, is acceptable if policy or technical limits call for it, although the memo notes that a mechanism doing none of these is not of much use. One peer may require stronger protection than the other can provide, which prevents perfect interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks for a security mechanism by name. The server accepts or refuses it, and if it accepts, the two sides exchange whatever data the mechanism needs. That exchange produces a security association, which may authenticate the client, the server, or neither, and which may or may not carry keys for protecting the data. The memo sets no policy, so each side decides what it insists on.

sections.title: AUTH and ADAT: Establishing a Security Association
sections.content:
AUTH takes a Telnet string naming a supported mechanism. The string is case-insensitive, and its values must be registered with IANA, except that values beginning with X- are reserved for local use. The reply codes say exactly why a request failed: 500 if the server does not recognize the AUTH command at all, which is what the large deployed base of non-security-aware servers sends for any unknown command; 502 if the server recognizes AUTH but does not implement the security extensions; 504 if the server does not understand the named mechanism; 534 if the server is not willing to accept that mechanism; 431 if the server is not able to accept it, for instance because a required resource is unavailable; 334 if the server is willing and requires security data; and 234 if the server is willing and needs none.

Accepting AUTH removes any state left over from earlier FTP security commands, and the server must then require the user to reauthorize, which means reissuing some or all of USER, PASS and ACCT. Some servers allow AUTH to be reissued in order to establish a new authentication.

ADAT carries the security data itself. Its argument is a Telnet string holding base 64 encoded security data, and the data is specific to the mechanism named by the preceding AUTH. When the server replies with a success code it may also return data to the client in a string of the form ADAT=base64data in the text part of the reply.

Together, AUTH and ADAT let the client and server run an arbitrary security protocol. The exchange has to carry enough information for both sides to know which optional features the other supports: if the client cannot decrypt, the server must find out so that it does not send encrypted command channel replies. The memo strongly recommends that the mechanism provide sequencing on the command channel, so that commands are not deleted, reordered or replayed.

The reply codes for ADAT are 503 if the server has not yet received an AUTH, or if a previous exchange finished and the security state was not reset with a new AUTH; 501 if the argument cannot be base 64 decoded; 535 if the server rejects the data, for instance because a checksum failed; 335 if the server accepts it but needs more; and 235 if the server accepts it and the exchange is complete. If ADAT returns an error the exchange fails and the client must reset its internal security state, and if the two sides lose step the client must reset the server's security state as well.

Section 9 of the memo gives a state diagram for the whole flow. It starts at an unauthenticated state on a new connection, moves to a state that needs security data when the server answers AUTH with 334, loops there while the server answers ADAT with 335, and reaches the authenticated state either on 234 for AUTH or on 235 for ADAT. From the authenticated state the login commands USER, PASS and ACCT continue towards the authorized state.
sections.plainLanguage: AUTH names the security mechanism to use, and the server's reply code says whether it accepted and whether it needs more data. ADAT then carries the mechanism's data back and forth, in blocks, until both sides have what they need. The exchange is what produces the security association, and it can be as simple as a key agreement that authenticates nobody.

sections.title: Protecting the Data and Command Channels
sections.content:
PBSZ negotiates the buffer size. Its argument is a decimal integer giving the maximum size, in bytes, of the encoded data blocks to be sent or received during a file transfer, and it may not exceed what fits in a 32-bit unsigned integer. There is no default size: the client must send PBSZ before its first PROT. PBSZ must follow a successful security data exchange. A server that cannot parse the argument, or find a value that fits in 32 bits, replies 501; a server with no completed exchange replies 503; otherwise it must reply 200, and if the client's size is too large it must use a string of the form PBSZ=number in the reply text to give a smaller size. When both sides give a size, the smaller one is used.

PROT sets the protection level for the data channel. Its argument is a single Telnet character: C for Clear, S for Safe, E for Confidential and P for Private. Clear carries the raw file data with no security applied, Safe adds integrity protection, Confidential adds confidentiality protection, and Private adds both. If no level is specified, the default is Clear. A mechanism need not offer every level, and may give more protection than a level requires. PROT must follow a successful PBSZ. The server replies 504 for a level it does not understand, 536 for a level the current mechanism does not support, 503 when no PBSZ has been done, 534 when it is not willing to accept the level, 431 when it is not able to, and otherwise 200 to accept it.

CCC, the clear command channel, takes no argument. Its purpose is to let a site authenticate its users without integrity checking every later command, for instance where IP security already authenticates the hosts and protects the TCP stream. The risk is that an attacker could then insert a command on the control stream and the server would have no way of knowing it was invalid, so once a security data exchange has succeeded the memo requires integrity protection, using MIC or ENC and the 631 or 632 replies, until CCC turns that requirement off. The CCC command itself must be integrity protected. Once CCC succeeds, a command that is not protected must have an unprotected reply too, so that clients without protection support can still be served. CCC must follow a successful security data exchange. The server replies 533 if the command was not integrity protected, 534 if it is not willing to turn the requirement off, and otherwise 200.

MIC, CONF and ENC send a command inside a protected wrapper. MIC carries a base 64 encoded safe message from the mechanism's message integrity procedure, CONF carries a base 64 encoded confidential message from its confidentiality procedure, and ENC carries a base 64 encoded private message from its integrity and confidentiality procedure. The server decodes and verifies the message and then interprets it as an FTP command; an end-of-line code is optional, and if present it must be a Telnet end-of-line code rather than a local one.

These three commands must follow a successful security data exchange. The server replies 502 if it requires CCC to be the first command after the exchange and does not implement the protection commands at all; 501 if the argument cannot be base 64 decoded; 503 if no exchange has completed, or if the mechanism supports integrity and the server requires CCC; 537 if the current security mechanism does not support the command; 535 if the command is rejected, for instance because a checksum failed; and 533 if the server is not willing to accept it, for instance because policy requires privacy or because a CONF command arrived before a CCC command. A server may require every command to be protected, in which case it answers 533 to anything other than MIC, CONF and ENC.

Section 8 gives the syntax of all seven commands. The mechanism name and the base 64 data are plain strings, the protection code is one of C, S, E or P, and the buffer size is any decimal integer from 1 to (2^32)-1. Section 10 fixes the base 64 encoding: it is the printable encoding of RFC 1421 without line breaks, using a 64-character subset of International Alphabet IA5 so that six bits fit in each printable character, with the character = used for padding. Because the encodings in ADAT, MIC, CONF and ENC and in the 63z replies may be arbitrarily long, the whole line has to be read before it can be processed, and case must not be ignored when reading it.
sections.plainLanguage: Four more commands turn the protection on. PBSZ agrees how large an encoded block may be. PROT says how the file data should be protected: in the clear, with a check that it was not altered, encrypted, or both. MIC, CONF and ENC wrap a single command in a protected envelope. CCC switches off the requirement to protect commands at all, for sites whose network already does that job.

sections.title: Data Channel Encapsulation
sections.content:
When a transfer is protected, the sender and receiver have to agree on how the protected bytes sit on the data connection. The sender applies all protection services after the transformations associated with the representation type, the file structure and the transfer mode have been performed, and the data is treated as a byte stream for the purposes of protection.

The sender takes the input byte stream and breaks it into blocks such that each block, once encoded by the mechanism's procedure, is no larger than the buffer size negotiated with PBSZ. Each block is encoded and then sent with the length of the encoded block prepended as a four byte unsigned integer, most significant byte first. When the end of the file is reached, the sender encodes a block of zero bytes and sends that final block before closing the data connection.

The recipient reads the four byte length, reads that many bytes of data, then decodes and verifies the block with the mechanism's own procedure, and repeats until a block encoding a zero byte buffer arrives, which marks the end of the encoded byte stream. The recipient then applies the transformations for the representation type, the file structure and the transfer mode to the resulting byte stream. When block transfer mode is used, the sender's cleartext buffer size is independent of the block size.

The memo flags a weakness here. Because the authentication checks are performed on individual blocks rather than on the file as a whole, it is possible for an insertion attack to insert blocks into the stream, that is to replay them, that authenticate correctly but corrupt the file without the receiver noticing. The specific security mechanism used should therefore include means of protecting against such attacks. The memo says that many of the GSS-API mechanisms usable with the specification in its Appendix I, and the Kerberos mechanism in its Appendix II, do so.

The server answers 534 to a STOR, STOU, RETR, LIST, NLST or APPE command if the current protection level is below the level its security requirements dictate for that transfer. If any data protection service fails at the server end at any time during the transfer, including an attempt to send a buffer larger than the negotiated maximum, the server sends 535 to the same data transfer command.
sections.plainLanguage: Protected file data is sent as a series of encoded blocks. Each block is written to the connection with a four byte length in front of it, and the receiver reads that length, decodes the block and checks it. A final empty block marks the end of the file. The memo warns that checking each block separately leaves room for an attacker to replay an old block, so the security mechanism has to deal with that.

sections.title: New FTP Reply Codes
sections.content:
The memo adds reply codes in two groups. The first group are new codes made necessary by the new commands: 232 for a user logged in and authorized by a security data exchange, 234 for a security data exchange that is complete, 235 for a security data exchange that completed successfully, optionally carrying security data as ADAT=base64data, 334 for a requested mechanism that is accepted and includes security data for the client to build its next command, 335 for security data that is acceptable but more is required, 336 for a username that is okay with a password still needed and a challenge in the reply text, 431 for an unavailable resource needed to process security, 533 for a command protection level denied for policy reasons, 534 for a request denied for policy reasons, 535 for a failed security check such as a hash or a sequence, 536 for a requested PROT level the mechanism does not support, and 537 for a command protection level the security mechanism does not support.

The second group is a new reply type for protected replies, written 6yz. There are three of them: 631 for an integrity protected reply, 632 for a reply with both confidentiality and integrity protection, and 633 for a confidentiality protected reply. The text part of each is a Telnet string holding a base 64 encoded safe, private or confidential message respectively, and the client decodes and verifies it. How a failure to decode or verify is handled is left to the implementation. A protected reply may only be sent once a security data exchange has succeeded.

A protected reply may be multiline. In that case the plaintext reply is broken into fragments, each fragment is protected and base 64 encoded in turn, and each becomes a separate line of the multiline reply. There need not be any correspondence between the line breaks in the plaintext and those in the encoded reply, and Telnet end-of-line codes must appear in the plaintext of the encoded reply except for the final one, which is optional. The formatting is stricter than the continuation rules of RFC 959: every line before the last is the reply code, a hyphen immediately after it, and then a base 64 encoded fragment.

Section 8.2 lists the reply codes that each command may return, which is the practical reference for an implementation. Any security command can also return 500, 501, 502, 533 or 421, and any FTP command can return a reply code encapsulated in a 631, 632 or 633 reply once a security data exchange has completed successfully.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds a set of reply codes for the new commands, including 234 and 235 when the security exchange ends and 336 when the server wants a challenge before the password. It also adds a new kind of reply, the 6yz type, where 631 means protected against alteration, 632 means encrypted and protected, and 633 means encrypted.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Policy
sections.content:
The memo says the whole document is about security considerations for FTP, and makes one specific limitation explicit: third party file transfers cannot be secured using these extensions. A security context cannot be established between two servers, because there is no control connection between servers over which to pass ADAT tokens. Further work in this area is deferred.

Section 7 gives recommendations rather than requirements. Once a security data exchange has taken place, a server should require all commands to be protected, with integrity and confidentiality, and should protect all replies. A reply should use the same level of protection as the command that produced it, including the replies that report the failure of a MIC, CONF or ENC command. Requiring AUTH and ADAT to be protected is not meaningful, because they are what set the security state up, but requiring PROT and PBSZ to be protected is meaningful and useful. The memo does not recommend using CCC, but defines it so that implementations which want that behaviour can interoperate.

A client should encrypt the PASS command whenever possible, and it is reasonable for a server to refuse a PASS command that is not encrypted if the server knows encryption is available. Although no security command has to be implemented, an implementation is recommended to provide all the commands it can, given the mechanisms it supports and the policy of the site, export controls being the example the memo gives.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo cannot secure a transfer that runs from one server to another, because there is no control connection between servers to carry the security tokens. Its other advice is a set of recommendations: protect every command and reply once the security exchange is done, encrypt the password, and implement every command that the site's policy allows.

items.title: AUTH
items.text: Names the security mechanism the client wants to use.

items.title: ADAT
items.text: Carries a block of base 64 encoded security data.

items.title: PBSZ
items.text: Negotiates the largest encoded data block for the transfer.

items.title: PROT
items.text: Sets the protection level of the data channel.

items.title: CCC
items.text: Turns off the requirement to protect the command channel.

items.title: MIC
items.text: Sends a command with integrity protection only.

items.title: CONF
items.text: Sends a command with confidentiality protection only.

items.title: ENC
items.text: Sends a command with integrity and confidentiality protection.

data.title: FTP security commands and arguments
data.code:
AUTH <SP> <mechanism-name> <CRLF>
ADAT <SP> <base64data> <CRLF>
PROT <SP> <prot-code> <CRLF>
PBSZ <SP> <decimal-integer> <CRLF>
MIC <SP> <base64data> <CRLF>
CONF <SP> <base64data> <CRLF>
ENC <SP> <base64data> <CRLF>

<mechanism-name> ::= <string>
<base64data> ::= <string>
<prot-code> ::= C | S | E | P
<decimal-integer> ::= any decimal integer from 1 to (2^32)-1

columns: Protection applied to the data channel

cells: Raw file data, with no security applied. This is the default.
The data is integrity and confidentiality protected.

items.label: Logged in
items.desc: User logged in, authorized by the security data exchange.

items.label: Exchange complete with data
items.desc: The exchange completed successfully. May carry ADAT=base64data.

items.label: Send security data
items.desc: The mechanism is accepted and the reply carries data for the client to use.

items.label: More data needed
items.desc: The security data is acceptable and more is required.

items.label: Challenge
items.desc: Username okay, password needed. The reply text carries the challenge.

items.label: Resource unavailable
items.desc: Some unavailable resource is needed to process security.

items.label: Denied by policy
items.desc: Command protection level denied for policy reasons.

items.label: Security check failed
items.desc: Failed security check, such as a hash or a sequence.

items.label: Level unsupported
items.desc: Requested PROT level is not supported by the mechanism.

items.label: Command unsupported
items.desc: Command protection level is not supported by the security mechanism.

items.label: Protected reply
items.desc: Integrity protected reply. The text holds a base 64 encoded safe message.

items.label: Protected reply
items.desc: Confidentiality and integrity protected reply. The text holds a base 64 encoded private message.

items.label: Protected reply
items.desc: Confidentiality protected reply. The text holds a base 64 encoded confidential message.
